title: EU imposes 9.5% anti-dumping duty on Indian cold-rolled steel; Tata Steel shares slide
intro: Trade friction with Europe leads today's edition. According to The Hindu BusinessLine, the European Commission on November 16 imposed a 9.5% anti-dumping duty on certain cold-rolled flat steel imports from India, covering Tata Steel and JSW Steel among others, and Tata Steel shares slid nearly 2%. The home market offers little relief. Shanghai Metals Market describes domestic steel as under pressure, and steel stocks were among the day's top losers. There are firmer signals elsewhere. Imported scrap offers have risen, core industries output grew 10.9% in October, construction has begun on JSW Steel's Paradip plant, and the government is to examine steel levies outside GST. Much of today's material comes from headlines alone, and we note where detail is missing.

marketOverview: Shanghai Metals Market's weekly review says India's domestic steel market remains under pressure. The publisher's excerpt does not give finished steel price levels, volumes or causes. Input markets point in different directions. According to kalkine.co.uk, imported scrap offers rose about 2.4% to $360-362 a tonne, which the headline attributes to thin arrivals and a semi-finished steel uptick. BigMint reports that Jindal SAW cut iron ore pellet offers by INR 400/t ($4/t) in Kandla, though the new level is not stated. In equities, Upstox lists JSW Steel and Tata Steel among the top losers during a global selloff.

sections.title: Steel Price Developments
sections.summary: Shanghai Metals Market reports that India's domestic steel market remains under pressure, but its excerpt gives no price levels. kalkine.co.uk says imported scrap offers rose about 2.4% to $360-362 a tonne, helped by thin arrivals and a semi-finished steel uptick. BigMint reports a reduction of INR 400/t ($4/t) in Jindal SAW's pellet offers in Kandla. Taken together, these reports point to firmer scrap and softer pellets, against a weak market for finished steel.

analysis: Analysis: Today's material shows Indian steel under pressure from two sides. Abroad, the EU's 9.5% duty on certain cold-rolled flat products could narrow one export outlet for the larger integrated producers. If exporters redirect that tonnage to India, it could add to supply in a domestic market that Shanghai Metals Market already describes as under pressure. The excerpts give no export volumes, however, so the scale of any diversion cannot be judged. The government's review of levies outside GST suggests policymakers recognise the competitiveness concern, but its scope is unknown. On costs, signals are mixed. Firmer imported scrap offers could squeeze electric-furnace producers if finished prices stay weak. Softer pellet offers in Kandla may offer some relief to other mills. Over the longer term, Tata Steel's preparations for 2030 mine auctions and Jindal's remarks on coking coal show producers trying to secure their raw materials. Meanwhile, the start of construction at Paradip indicates that capacity expansion is continuing despite near-term weakness. Readers should treat these readings cautiously, as much of the material consists of headlines without detail.
